title: Entity Set
description: Distinguish an entity type from its current population, define membership clearly, and report sets without confusing shared attributes or changing relationships with identity.
notes:
## A population of modeled occurrences

An entity set is a collection of entity occurrences sharing a modeled type at the relevant state. The Student set can contain the currently recorded student occurrences. Each member has the roles and identifying rules specified for that type, while individual values can differ. Student seventeen and Student twenty-four are two members, even if they share a name or programme.

An entity occurrence is one identifiable member; the set is the collection. In introductory diagram discussions, the named rectangle often stands for the type and its set of occurrences. Keep those two ideas understandable rather than treating a category name as one person or treating one example member as the whole population. The common definition and current members answer different questions.

## Type definitions remain meaningful when empty

A Student type can be defined before admissions records have been loaded. Its current set can then be empty while identifying rules and attributes remain meaningful. Adding the first student changes membership, not the existence of the type's definition. An empty set has no current members; it does not acquire one placeholder person merely to make the diagram valid.

A set can also become empty after legitimate state changes, depending on the modeled lifecycle. Whether records should be retained historically is a separate domain policy. Do not infer that removing current membership means deleting every historical fact about the occurrence. Current active students, all recorded students, and students who ever enrolled can be different populations over related data.

## Membership needs a documented boundary

What does the Student set include: admitted students, currently active students, alumni, or every institutional person record with a student role? Different answers lead to different queries and lifecycle decisions. A status column can distinguish roles in one broader relation, while another design may use separate relations or views. Define the intended collection before counting or filtering its members.

The boundary can depend on time. A report for the current term differs from a report over all historical enrollments. Use the required dates, statuses, or relationship facts explicitly rather than relying on a vague title such as current students. A familiar set name does not tell a query which records qualify unless the model or report contract states that rule.

## Common attributes do not require equal values

Members of a modeled type share attribute roles, not necessarily the same attribute values. Two students can have different programmes, names, and optional contact details while both belong to Student. A missing optional phone number does not remove the phone role from the type or automatically remove the student from the set. The absence policy follows the actual attribute definition.

Likewise, two entity sets can use an attribute called email without becoming the same set. Student.email and Faculty.email occupy roles within different definitions or role mappings. Shared spelling alone does not establish shared identity, membership, or a foreign-key relationship. Interpret attributes in their modeled scope rather than equating every column with the same name across a database.

## Sets can overlap under role modeling

One person can be both a student and a teaching assistant if the domain permits those roles. Whether the design represents that through overlapping entity sets, subtypes, or a shared Person identity depends on the requirements. It is incorrect to infer that all named sets must be disjoint merely because diagrams draw separate rectangles.

Conversely, two rows with the same name in Student and Faculty do not prove they describe the same person. A shared identifying policy or explicit relationship must establish that connection. Role overlap is about real intended identities, not accidental equality of descriptive labels. Keep identity evidence and participation evidence distinct when designing a cross-role report.

## Relationships connect members of sets

An enrollment relationship links particular student and course-offering members. A single student can participate in several enrollments while remaining one member of Student. An entity set's size and the number of related participation facts are therefore different measurements. A join can display one student several times without increasing the conceptual number of student entities.

Cardinality in entity-relationship notation can describe allowed relationship multiplicity rather than the exact current number of entity members. A one-to-many relationship permits certain participation patterns; it does not assert that every parent currently has many children. Read minimum and maximum participation rules separately from actual fixture counts and the size of an entity population.

## Mapping to relations is useful but qualified

A simple strong entity set commonly maps to a relation containing one tuple for each recorded occurrence. Attributes become appropriate columns and identifying rules become supported constraints. This is a helpful introductory mapping. More elaborate models can use multiple relations for multivalued properties, subtypes, history, or other structures without redefining the conceptual entity as a physical storage artifact.

A weak entity set also maps to a relation with a complete implemented identity. In a conventional identifying mapping, that identity includes its owner's key and a local discriminator. Saying a weak entity table has no primary key at all would be misleading. The distinction concerns dependence on an owner for conceptual identification, not whether the final relational table can enforce a complete combined key.

## Query the intended member population

A query can list a named population through an explicit predicate and projection. Suppose active status defines the report's current membership. The query should filter that status while keeping identifiers so two students with the same name remain separate members. A narrower projection of distinct names would describe names represented in the population rather than the population itself.

```sql
SELECT student_id, student_name
FROM students
WHERE status = 'active'
ORDER BY student_id;
```

This report intentionally excludes inactive records even if the broader stored Student relation retains them. The result contract must say whether it lists current active members or all recorded students. A label alone cannot reconcile an implementation that counts one population and describes it as the other.

## Aggregates can preserve empty categories

A Programme catalogue can define categories even when no current active student belongs to one. A report asking for every programme and its active-student count should preserve those categories and show zero where appropriate. Starting from active students alone omits empty programmes entirely, which answers a different question about represented programmes.

When using a preserving join, place the active-member condition where it does not discard unmatched programme rows. Count a nonmissing student identity rather than every preserved output row. If a programme has only inactive students, its active count should still be zero. Include that fixture alongside a programme with no students so both population boundaries are tested directly.

## Membership changes are not always identity changes

A student can become inactive or join another programme while retaining the same identity. That changes membership of a filtered active or programme-specific set without creating a different student occurrence. A historical report may need the earlier membership, so the data model must record the required history rather than expecting current status to reconstruct past states automatically.

Deleting an occurrence from a stored table is a more consequential operation than excluding it from a report. It can affect references and retained facts. Distinguish those operations in explanations: WHERE controls the returned population; it does not remove the source entity or automatically enforce lifecycle policy. Query semantics, data modification, and authorization remain separate concerns.

## Validate population and representation together

Use repeated names, active and inactive students, an empty type population, a programme with no students, and a programme containing only inactive students. Confirm which members appear and what each count measures. A single perfect example can hide a wrong filter location or an accidental distinct-name interpretation because several different queries happen to agree on that narrow fixture.

Entity sets are useful when their common definition, membership boundary, and identities are explicit. Keep the conceptual population distinct from one entity, one descriptive-value set, and one joined report. A SQL mapping can demonstrate these distinctions on synthetic fixtures without proving every possible ER transformation or production policy. The goal is a clear account of which occurrences belong, how they are identified, and what a particular query reports about them.

questions.question_text: What is an entity set?
options: A single, uniquely identified real-world object
The modeled collection of current occurrences sharing an entity type and its attribute roles
A rule limiting the values of an attribute
A diagram showing cardinalities between entities
questions.explanation: Common attribute roles do not imply equal values across members.

questions.question_text: In an ER diagram, how is an entity set typically drawn?
options: As a diamond
As an oval
As a rectangle
As a double rectangle
questions.explanation: A rectangle represents an entity set (a double rectangle is reserved for weak entity sets).

questions.question_text: For a simple strong-entity relational mapping, which correspondence is a useful introductory analogy?
options: Entity = table, Entity set = row
Entity = row (tuple), Entity set = table (relation)
Entity = column, Entity set = table
Entity = database, Entity set = schema
questions.explanation: A simple mapping often uses one tuple per occurrence and a relation for the set; more elaborate mappings need not be one physical table per conceptual entity.

questions.question_text: Can an entity set validly exist with zero current entities in it?
options: No, an entity set must always contain at least one entity
Yes; the type definition remains meaningful while its current member population is empty
Only weak entity sets can be empty
Only if it has no attributes
questions.explanation: The definition and its current population must be distinguished.

questions.question_text: Both 'Student' and 'Faculty' entity sets have an attribute called 'Email'. What does this imply?
options: They are actually the same entity set
Attribute names can be reused across different entity sets; they remain distinct sets
This is not allowed in the ER model
One of them must be a weak entity set
questions.explanation: Different entity sets can share attribute names; what makes them distinct is their overall structure and identity, not unique attribute names.

questions.question_text: Which of these statements distinguishes an entity from an entity set most precisely?
options: An entity has attributes; an entity set does not
An entity is one occurrence; an entity set is the named collection/category of all such occurrences
An entity set can only contain one entity
There is no meaningful distinction in practice
questions.explanation: This instance-vs-category distinction is the essence of entity vs. entity set.

questions.question_text: A weak entity set differs from a (strong) entity set primarily because:
options: It has more attributes
Its conceptual identification depends on an owner and local discriminator rather than an independent complete identifier
It cannot be drawn in an ER diagram
It never has any attributes
questions.explanation: A conventional relational weak-entity mapping can still have a complete composite primary key including the owner key.

questions.question_text: When converting ER to a relational schema, what typically happens to a strong entity set?
options: It is discarded and merged into its relationships
It becomes a table whose columns are its attributes and whose rows are its entities
It becomes a foreign key in another table
It becomes an index
questions.explanation: A strong entity set maps directly to a table: attributes become columns, and each entity instance becomes a row.

questions.question_text: Do common student attribute roles require every student to share the same programme value?
options: Yes; otherwise they are different types automatically
No; values can differ across members
Only for empty sets
Only if names repeat
questions.explanation: Type structure and current property values differ.

questions.question_text: Can Student and Faculty both use an email attribute without being the same set?
options: No; shared names merge sets
Only if email is numeric
Yes; names are interpreted within their modeled roles
Only if neither has keys
questions.explanation: Attribute spelling does not establish identity or membership equivalence.

questions.question_text: Must all named entity sets be disjoint?
options: Yes; separate rectangles prove disjointness
Only empty sets overlap
No; the model can permit overlapping roles
Only tables without keys overlap
questions.explanation: Role overlap is an explicit modeling decision.

questions.question_text: What establishes that one person belongs to both Student and Faculty?
options: The same displayed name alone
The same row position
A similar email label alone
The model’s shared identity or explicit relationship evidence
questions.explanation: Descriptive coincidence is not enough.

questions.question_text: Why can a student appear several times in an enrollment report?
options: Several participation facts concern that one student
The entity set automatically gained clones
Every repeated name is invalid
Every join creates new students
questions.explanation: Joined result grain differs from student identity count.

questions.question_text: What does one-to-many notation primarily describe?
options: An exact current row count
Allowed relationship multiplicity
The number of attributes
Mandatory many children for every parent
questions.explanation: Participation rules and current populations differ.

questions.question_text: What happens when a student becomes inactive under an active-membership report?
options: Their internal identity must change
Every enrollment is automatically deleted
They can leave that filtered population while retaining identity
The Student definition disappears
questions.explanation: Membership predicates can change without entity replacement.

questions.question_text: Which query would report names rather than student occurrences?
options: SELECT student_id, student_name
SELECT the unique identifier
A lookup by student_id
SELECT DISTINCT student_name
questions.explanation: Distinct descriptive values can collapse different member identities.

questions.question_text: Why begin a zero-inclusive programme report from programmes?
options: It preserves defined categories with no active members
It makes every student active
It deletes inactive rows
It creates new programmes
questions.explanation: Starting only from active members omits empty categories.

questions.question_text: Where should a preserving join apply its active-student eligibility without losing programmes?
options: Only in a WHERE that rejects unmatched rows
In the join condition or an equivalent preserving formulation
By deleting programme identifiers
By counting all rows regardless of status
questions.explanation: The population predicate must preserve the requested parent categories.

questions.question_text: Does excluding a row through WHERE delete the source entity?
options: Yes; WHERE always writes
Only if sorted
No; it changes the returned population
Only if no rows remain
questions.explanation: Retrieval filtering differs from data modification.

questions.question_text: What must a weak entity’s conventional relational mapping still provide?
options: No identifying constraint at all
Only a display row number
A key on every descriptive name
A complete implemented identity, often owner key plus discriminator
questions.explanation: Identification dependence does not mean an unidentifiable final table.

coding_problems.title: List the explicitly defined active student population
coding_problems.task: Return student_id and student_name only for status active. Keep different students with the same name.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, student_name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL, status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL);
constraints: The report defines current membership as status active; stored inactive records remain in the broader source.
edge_cases: No active student yields an empty listing.
hints: Retain the identifying value in the projection.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT student_id, student_name FROM students WHERE status = 'active' ORDER BY student_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The predicate defines the requested population without changing stored identity or deleting inactive records.

coding_problems.title: Count active members while retaining empty programmes
coding_problems.task: For every programme return programme_id and active_students. Count only active student members and keep programmes with no active students as zero.
coding_problems.schema_sql:
CREATE TABLE programmes (programme_id INT PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE students (student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, programme_id INT NOT NULL, status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO programmes VALUES (1),(2),(3),(4); INSERT INTO students VALUES (1,1,'active'),(2,1,'active'),(3,2,'inactive'),(4,3,'active');
constraints: Student references match the supplied programme catalogue; native FK enforcement is outside these temporary mirrors.
edge_cases: A programme can contain only inactive members.
A programme can have no stored students at all.
hints: Preserve programmes while applying student eligibility in the join.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT p.programme_id, COUNT(s.student_id) AS active_students FROM programmes p LEFT JOIN students s ON s.programme_id = p.programme_id AND s.status = 'active' GROUP BY p.programme_id ORDER BY p.programme_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The preserving join retains every catalogue category, while the join predicate defines eligible members without discarding unmatched programmes.

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO programmes VALUES (2),(1); INSERT INTO students VALUES (1,1,'inactive');
